docs.title: openmm-opes
docs.text:
On-the-fly Probability Enhanced Sampling (OPES) for OpenMM.

OPES is an enhanced sampling method that builds its bias from an on-the-fly estimate of the probability distribution along a few collective variables, instead of accumulating repulsive hills as metadynamics does. The bias soon becomes nearly static, so free energies converge quickly and reweighting is simple. It needs only an expected barrier height, a deposition stride and a kernel bandwidth. This package implements OPES in pure Python on top of OpenMM, in the spirit of openmm.app.Metadynamics, and is validated against PLUMED's OPES_METAD and OPES_METAD_EXPLORE.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• OPES and OPES-explore, with fixed, adaptive or warm-up bandwidths and on-the-fly kernel compression.
  • OPES and OPES-explore combined (OPES_COM), as a single CombinedOPES sampler.
  • Multiple walkers sharing one bias through a directory.
  • Several samplers on one simulation, with extra biases folded into the reweighting.
  • Reweighting tools: the reweighting constant c(t), and PLUMED's rct as a convergence check.
  • Smoothing-corrected free energy surfaces.
  • Periodic, unbounded or reflective collective variables, one to three of them.
  • Checkpoints through getState and setState.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install openmm-opes

It needs Python 3.11 or later and OpenMM 8.1 or later. OpenMM can also come from conda-forge:

conda install -c conda-forge openmm
pip install openmm-opes

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
from openmm import unit
from openmm_opes import OPES

sampler = OPES(
    system,
    [phi, psi],  # openmm.app.BiasVariable objects
    temperature=300 * unit.kelvin,
    barrier=40 * unit.kilojoules_per_mole,
    frequency=500,
    varianceFrequency=50,
)
sampler.step(simulation, 1_000_000)
fes = sampler.getFreeEnergy(correctSmoothing=True)

The quickstart has a complete runnable example and the main options. The theory page shows how the code maps onto the published equations and where it departs from them. The benchmarks compare openmm-opes with PLUMED's OPES and with OpenMM's metadynamics, against a reference surface for alanine dipeptide.

docs.title: Origin
docs.text: This library packages and hardens the prototype implementation developed in craabreu/opes-simulations, porting its OPES and OnlineKDE classes into a tested, documented package.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. M. Invernizzi and M. Parrinello, Rethinking Metadynamics: From Bias Potentials to Probability Distributions, J. Phys. Chem. Lett. 11, 2731 (2020). doi:10.1021/acs.jpclett.0c00497
  2. M. Invernizzi and M. Parrinello, Exploration vs Convergence Speed in Adaptive-Bias Enhanced Sampling, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 18, 3988 (2022). doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00152
  3. D. Ray and V. Rizzi, Enhanced Sampling with Suboptimal Collective Variables: Reconciling Accuracy and Convergence Speed, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 58 (2025). doi:10.1021/acs.jctc.4c01231
  4. M. C. Jones, O. Linton and J. P. Nielsen, A Simple Bias Reduction Method for Density Estimation, Biometrika 82, 327 (1995).

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This example biases a single particle on the two-dimensional Müller-Brown potential along x and y, and recovers its free energy surface.

import numpy as np
import openmm as mm
from openmm import app, unit

from openmm_opes import OPES

KB = unit.MOLAR_GAS_CONSTANT_R.value_in_unit(
    unit.kilojoules_per_mole / unit.kelvin
)

muller_brown = (
    "-200*exp(-(x-1)^2-10*y^2)"
    " -100*exp(-x^2-10*(y-0.5)^2)"
    " -170*exp(-6.5*(0.5+x)^2+11*(x+0.5)*(y-1.5)-6.5*(y-1.5)^2)"
    " +15*exp(0.7*(1+x)^2+0.6*(x+1)*(y-1)+0.7*(y-1)^2)"
)

system = mm.System()
system.addParticle(1.0)
potential = mm.CustomExternalForce(muller_brown)
potential.addParticle(0, [])
system.addForce(potential)

variables = []
for expression, lo, hi in (("x", -1.5, 1.2), ("y", -0.2, 2.0)):
    force = mm.CustomExternalForce(expression)
    force.addParticle(0, [])
    variables.append(app.BiasVariable(force, lo, hi, 0.1, False, 101))

temperature = 1.0 / KB * unit.kelvin
sampler = OPES(
    system,
    variables,
    temperature,
    barrier=20 * unit.kilojoules_per_mole,
    frequency=500,
    varianceFrequency=50,
)

topology = app.Topology()
topology.addAtom("P", None, topology.addResidue("MOL", topology.addChain()))
integrator = mm.LangevinMiddleIntegrator(
    temperature, 10.0 / unit.picosecond, 0.005 * unit.picoseconds
)
simulation = app.Simulation(
    topology, system, integrator, mm.Platform.getPlatformByName("Reference")
)
simulation.context.setPositions([mm.Vec3(-0.5, 1.4, 0.0)])
simulation.context.setVelocitiesToTemperature(temperature)

sampler.step(simulation, 2_000_000)

fes = sampler.getFreeEnergy().value_in_unit(unit.kilojoules_per_mole)
fes -= fes.min()
print(f"{sampler.getNumKernels()} kernels, barrier {fes.max():.1f} kJ/mol")

getFreeEnergy() returns an array on the CV grid in which the last variable varies fastest. For two CVs, its shape is (ny, nx), so it can go straight to matplotlib.pyplot.contourf.

docs.title: Choosing the bandwidth
docs.text:
Both OPES papers recommend measuring the initial bandwidth in a short unbiased run. The sampler can do that for you:

sampler = OPES(..., varianceFrequency=50, warmupSteps=50_000)

No kernels are deposited during the first 50,000 steps. The CV variance measured over them sets the initial bandwidth, which is then held fixed.

To set the bandwidth yourself, pass varianceFrequency=None and give each variable a biasWidth. It is read as \(\sigma^{(0)}\), the standard deviation of the unbiased distribution, for both OPES and OPES-explore. OPES-explore kernels estimate the sampled distribution, which is \(\sqrt{\gamma}\) times wider, so they are deposited \(\sqrt{\gamma}\) times wider than biasWidth.

docs.title: Correcting the smoothing bias
docs.text:
Kernel smoothing makes steep basin walls too low and basin floors too high in the reported free energy. To remove that bias, ask for it:

fes = sampler.getFreeEnergy(correctSmoothing=True)

The correction also lowers the noise of a single run. It needs kernels that are narrow compared with the basins, so it can make things worse very early in a run, while the kernels are still wide. The bias itself is never changed. See the theory page for how it works.

docs.title: OPES combined with OPES-explore
docs.text:
CombinedOPES runs OPES and OPES-explore together on the same collective variables: the combined algorithm of Ray and Rizzi, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 58 (2025), often called OPES_COM. The explore bias keeps pushing the system out of its minima, which helps when the CVs are suboptimal, while the OPES bias converges the free energy. Each component has its own barrier, and the paper recommends an explore barrier below the OPES one.

from openmm_opes import CombinedOPES

sampler = CombinedOPES(system, variables, temperature, barrier=40,
                       exploreBarrier=20, frequency=500, varianceFrequency=50)
sampler.step(simulation, 1_000_000)
fes = sampler.getFreeEnergy()

Neither component estimates the unbiased distribution on its own, because each one's samples also feel the other's bias. getFreeEnergy() therefore returns a third estimate, which reweights every sample by the total bias. getComponentBiases() and getComponentBiasEnergies(context) give the two parts separately.

docs.title: Multiple walkers
docs.text:
Several simulations can share one bias. Give each one its own sampler with the same settings, point them all at the same directory, and give each a stable walker id:

sampler = OPES(system, variables, temperature, barrier, 500, 50,
               saveFrequency=5000, biasDir="walkers", walkerId=rank)

Every saveFrequency steps, which must be a multiple of the deposition frequency, each walker writes its own kernels to the directory and reads in everyone else's. The walkers can run as separate processes, or on separate machines that share a file system. A stable walkerId lets a restarted walker take back its own file, instead of leaving the old one behind as a phantom extra walker. CombinedOPES takes the same options and keeps each component's files in a subdirectory of its own.

docs.title: Several samplers at once
docs.text:
More generally, several samplers can bias the same simulation, as several OPES actions can in one PLUMED input. Each deposits kernels on its own schedule and weights them by its own bias only. Create them all on the same System and advance the simulation with OPES.stepTogether. For example, here is an OPES sampler on two CVs alongside an OPES-explore sampler on the first one:

opes = OPES(system, [cv1, cv2], temperature, 55, 500, 50)
explore = OPES(system, [cv1Copy], temperature, 30, 500, 50, exploreMode=True)
simulation = app.Simulation(topology, system, integrator)
...
OPES.stepTogether(simulation, [opes, explore], 1_000_000)

Each sampler's bias force takes ownership of its variables' forces, so give every sampler its own BiasVariable objects. Because each sampler weights kernels by its own bias only, its getFreeEnergy() is still biased by the others. To remove them, pass them as extra biases, described next, or reweight with the sum of the biases that getBiasEnergy(simulation.context) returns for each sampler.

docs.title: Other biases and c(t)
docs.text:
When other biases act on the simulation, such as a restraint you want removed from the free energy or another sampler, pass them as extraBias, like PLUMED's EXTRA_BIAS. Each sample is then weighted by all of them, so getFreeEnergy() removes them too. Items can be force groups, Force objects or other samplers:

restraint.setForceGroup(5)  # give it a group of its own
sampler = OPES(system, variables, temperature, barrier, 500, 50,
               extraBias=[restraint])

extraBias also works in explore mode, where it changes only the reweighted free energy. PLUMED offers EXTRA_BIAS for OPES_METAD only.

getCt() returns c(t), the constant that makes reweighting exact while the bias still changes: a sample taken at time t gets the weight exp(β[V_t(s) − c(t)]). The default estimate uses the current bias and the current density estimate. getCt("running") is PLUMED's rct. It lags behind the current bias, so treat it as PLUMED does: as a convergence diagnostic that levels off once the bias converges, not as a reweighting constant.

docs.title: The method as implemented
docs.text: Notation follows Invernizzi and Parrinello: \(\beta = 1/k_BT\), \(\gamma\) is the bias factor, and \(\mathbf{s}\) denotes the collective variables.

docs.title: The probability estimate
docs.text:
OPES estimates the unbiased distribution by weighted kernel density estimation,

\[P_n(\mathbf{s}) = \frac{\sum_k^n w_k\, G(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}_k)}{\sum_k^n w_k}, \qquad w_k = e^{\beta V_{k-1}(\mathbf{s}_k)}\]

with normalized Gaussian kernels \(G\), of height \(h = \prod_i (\sigma_i\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\). This is OnlineKDE.getLogPDF(). The weight comes from the bias energy read from the OPES force group before the new kernel is deposited, so it really is \(V_{k-1}\).

docs.title: Bandwidth
docs.text:
As the effective sample size \(N_{\text{eff}} = (\sum_{k=0}^n w_k)^2 / \sum_{k=0}^n w_k^2\), with \(w_0 = 1\), grows, Silverman's rule shrinks the bandwidths of new kernels:

\[\sigma_i^{(n)} = \sigma_i^{(0)}\left[N_{\text{eff}}^{(n)}(d+2)/4\right]^{-1/(d+4)}\]

There is no lower bound by default, as in PLUMED. The bias is tabulated on the CV grid and interpolated with splines, so kernels narrower than the grid spacing are not resolved in detail. This costs sampling efficiency, not correctness. The simulation feels exactly the tabulated bias, and kernels are weighted with that same bias, so the reweighted estimate stays unbiased. A floor would instead change the estimate itself, by keeping kernels wider than Silverman's rule prescribes. minBandwidth sets one if needed.

docs.title: Adaptive bandwidth
docs.text:
With a varianceFrequency, \(\sigma^{(0)}\) follows the CV variance measured on the fly, as an exponentially decaying mean over a window of \(\tau\) = statsWindowSize deposition strides. This follows Eqs. S1–S4 in the supporting information of Invernizzi and Parrinello's 2022 paper. The variance is that of the sampled distribution, so OPES divides it by \(\gamma\) to size its reweighted kernels, while OPES-explore uses it as is.

No kernel is deposited during the first \(\tau\) strides, so those samples are unbiased, and their variance is \(\gamma\) times smaller than that of a sampled distribution. When the wait ends, the squared deviations accumulated so far are multiplied by \(\gamma\), once. Later samples come from the biased run and enter unscaled. Without this step, the first kernels would be \(\sqrt{\gamma}\) times too narrow and the early bias spiky. The published equations omit it, but PLUMED's OPES_METAD and OPES_METAD_EXPLORE apply it at their first deposition.

docs.title: Warm-up bandwidth estimation
docs.text: Both OPES papers recommend measuring \(\sigma^{(0)}\) in a short unbiased run. Passing warmupSteps automates this. No kernels are deposited until that many steps have elapsed, so the CV variance measured over that span is genuinely unbiased. When warm-up ends, the variance is frozen. It is stored multiplied by \(\gamma\), because kernels are sized from a sampled-distribution variance by convention.

docs.title: Kernel compression
docs.text:
A new kernel closer than compressionThreshold to an existing one, in Mahalanobis distance, is merged into it, preserving total weight, mean and second moment. Compression keeps the number of kernels bounded, and that number is what makes \(|\Omega_n|\), below, estimable.

This merge rule differs on purpose from that of PLUMED's OPES_METAD, which weights the merged center and variance by kernel height, \(h = w/\prod_i \sigma_i\), and keeps \(h_1 + h_2\) as the merged height. When the two kernels have different bandwidths, as they do once Silverman's rule has shrunk the newer one, that rule does not conserve probability mass. Given the same weighted samples and bandwidths, both rules compress to about as many kernels. Against the uncompressed estimate, however, the mass-preserving merge is five to eight times more accurate: its mean absolute log-density error is 0.03–0.05, against 0.17–0.25. The height-weighted merge also inflates the total mass by 17–27%. The script is benchmarks/plumed/merge_accuracy.py. Biases built from the same samples therefore differ slightly from PLUMED's, by about 1 kJ/mol RMS in the tests there.

docs.title: Normalization
docs.text:
\(Z_n\) normalizes over the CV space explored so far:

\[Z_n = \frac{1}{|\Omega_n|}\int_{\Omega_n} P_n(\mathbf{s})\, d\mathbf{s}\]

It is approximated by an average over the compressed kernel centers, in OnlineKDE.getLogMeanDensity().

docs.title: The bias
docs.text:
\[V_n(\mathbf{s}) = \left(1 - \tfrac{1}{\gamma}\right)\frac{1}{\beta} \log\left(\frac{P_n(\mathbf{s})}{Z_n} + \epsilon\right)\]

Here, \(\epsilon = e^{-\beta\Delta E/(1-1/\gamma)}\) limits the bias to the barrier \(\Delta E\). This is OPES.getBias().

docs.title: OPES-explore
docs.text:
The explore variant estimates the sampled distribution instead, with uniform weights:

\[p^{\text{WT}}_n(\mathbf{s}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k^n G(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}_k), \qquad V_n(\mathbf{s}) = (\gamma-1)\frac{1}{\beta} \log\left(\frac{p^{\text{WT}}_n(\mathbf{s})}{Z_n} + \epsilon\right)\]

It explores faster and converges more slowly. In explore mode, getBias() reads the unweighted estimate; otherwise it reads the reweighted one. Because \(p^{\text{WT}}\) is about \(\sqrt{\gamma}\) times wider than \(P\), explore kernels start at \(\sqrt{\gamma}\,\sigma^{(0)}\), and a fixed biasWidth is still read as the unbiased \(\sigma^{(0)}\).

docs.title: OPES combined with OPES-explore
docs.text:
CombinedOPES follows Ray and Rizzi, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 58 (2025). Both components deposit a kernel at the same steps and CV values. The explore component builds its target estimate from the unweighted samples, which feel the total bias \(V^o + V^e\). The OPES component weights its kernels by its own bias only, \(w_k = e^{\beta V^o_{k-1}(\mathbf{s}_k)}\), so it estimates the distribution biased by \(V^e\), not the unbiased one. The unbiased estimate reweights every sample by the total bias,

\[P_n(\mathbf{s}) = \frac{\sum_k^n w_k\, G(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{s}_k)}{\sum_k^n w_k}, \qquad w_k = e^{\beta [V^o_{k-1}(\mathbf{s}_k) + V^e_{k-1}(\mathbf{s}_k)]}\]

which is the paper's Eq. 14, accumulated on the fly. Its kernels are sized as in the explore component's reweighted estimate. The two biases share one force, so the CVs are computed once per step. At each deposition, the explore term is switched off for one evaluation of the bias force group, to read \(V^o\) alone.

docs.title: Free energy
docs.text: getFreeEnergy() always uses the importance-sampling estimate, \(F_n = -\beta^{-1}\log P_n\). In standard OPES, the direct and reweighted routes are equivalent. In explore mode, they differ until convergence, and the reweighted one converges better.

docs.title: Smoothing correction
docs.text:
A kernel estimate is the true density convolved with the kernels, so to leading order it overshoots by \(\tfrac{1}{2}h^2\nabla^2 P\). In free energy terms, basin floors come out too high and steep walls too low. Silverman's rule narrows new kernels only slowly, and old kernels keep their width, so this bias fades slowly.

getFreeEnergy(correctSmoothing=True) removes it with the multiplicative correction of Jones, Linton and Nielsen, Biometrika 82, 327 (1995). A pilot estimate \(\tilde P\) uses the same kernels, broadened by pilotFactor. Each kernel's weight is divided by \(\tilde P\) at its center, so the reweighted samples follow the nearly flat ratio \(P/\tilde P\). Smoothing that ratio with the broad kernels costs little bias:

\[\hat P(\mathbf{s}) = \tilde P(\mathbf{s})\, \frac{\sum_k w_k\, \tilde G_k(\mathbf{s}) / \tilde P(\mathbf{s}_k)}{\sum_k w_k}\]

The bias drops to order \(h^4\), while the broad kernels keep the noise of a single run low. The product does not conserve probability locally, which would shift free energy differences between basins. So the result is rescaled to carry, over a few pilot widths, the same probability as the standard estimate.

For sixteen 50 ns runs of alanine dipeptide, these are the RMS errors against a reference surface, where the reference is below 5 kcal/mol, in kcal/mol:

Estimate Single run Average of 16 runs Standard 0.099 0.055 Corrected, pilotFactor=2 0.059 0.026

Free energy differences between basins were unchanged. The correction needs the broadened kernels to be narrow compared with the basins. Early in a run, while kernels are still wide, it can make the surface worse. It changes only the reported free energy, not the bias.

docs.title: Extra biases and c(t)
docs.text:
When other biases \(V_x\) act on the simulation, the kernel weights become \(w_k = e^{\beta [V_{k-1}(\mathbf{s}_k) + V_x(\mathbf{R}_k)]}\), so \(P_n\) estimates the distribution with every bias removed. The OPES bias itself is built from \(P_n\) as before.

For a bias that changes in time, reweighting a sample taken at time \(t\) by \(e^{\beta [V_t(\mathbf{s}) - c(t)]}\) is exact, with

\[c(t) = -\frac{1}{\beta}\ln \frac{\int P(\mathbf{s})\, e^{-\beta V_t(\mathbf{s})}\,d\mathbf{s}}{\int P(\mathbf{s})\,d\mathbf{s}}\]

getCt() evaluates this on the grid, with \(P_n\) in place of \(P\). It is unbiased once \(P_n\) is, but wrong while \(P_n\) still misses basins. getCt("running") is PLUMED's rct, \(\beta^{-1}\ln[(w_0 + \sum_k w_k) / (n + 1)]\): the mean weight of all samples so far, plus one fictitious sample under the initial flat bias, \(w_0 = e^{-\beta\Delta E}\). It lags behind the current bias, because it averages over past ones, and PLUMED advises against reweighting with it. Use it to check that the bias has converged. On alanine dipeptide, the current-bias estimate is the more accurate one after about 2 ns.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Two samplers drive simulations:

  • OPES: OPES and OPES-explore, biasing a simulation through one OpenMM force.
  • CombinedOPES: OPES and OPES-explore acting together on the same collective variables (OPES_COM).

Both are built on a kernel density estimate, whose classes can also be used directly or inspected:

  • OnlineKDE: a weighted kernel density estimate on a grid, with on-the-fly compression and the smoothing correction.
  • CVSpace: the grid, periodicity and reflective boundaries of the collective variables.
  • Kernel: one multivariate kernel with diagonal covariance.

docs.title: CombinedOPES
docs.text:
CombinedOPES(system, variables, temperature, barrier, exploreBarrier, frequency, varianceFrequency, biasFactor=None, exploreBiasFactor=None, bounded=False, saveFrequency=None, biasDir=None, walkerId=None, warmupSteps=None, compressionThreshold=1.0, useExistingBandwidths=True, kernelShape='gaussian', statsWindowSize=10, minBandwidth=None, extraBias=None)

OPES and OPES-explore biasing the same collective variables together.

Implements the combined algorithm of Ray and Rizzi, https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.4c01231, often called OPES_COM. Both components deposit a kernel at the same steps, at the same CV values:

  • the OPES component estimates its marginal distribution with weights exp(beta V_opes) from its own bias only (their Eq. 11), so that distribution is still biased by the explore component (Eq. 12);
  • the explore component estimates its target distribution from the unweighted samples (Eq. 8), which feel both biases.

The total bias is V_opes + V_explore. Neither component estimates the unbiased distribution by itself, so a third estimate reweights every sample by exp(beta (V_opes + V_explore)), the paper's Eq. 14, and getFreeEnergy returns it. Its kernels are sized as those of the explore component's reweighted estimate.

Both components share one bias force, so the CVs are computed once per step. To weight OPES kernels by the OPES bias alone, the explore part of the force is switched off for a single energy evaluation at each deposition step.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default system

The System to simulate. A CustomCVForce implementing the total bias is created and added to it.

required variables

The collective variables both components bias.

required temperature

The temperature at which the simulation is run.

required barrier

The barrier of the OPES component, Delta E_OPES.

required exploreBarrier

The barrier of the OPES-explore component, Delta E_EXPLORE. The paper finds systematic errors when it exceeds barrier, and a warning is issued in that case.

required frequency

Interval in time steps at which both components deposit a kernel.

required varianceFrequency

Interval in time steps at which to update the CV variance, or None for a fixed bandwidth taken from each variable's biasWidth. See OPES.

required biasFactor

The OPES bias factor. Defaults to barrier / kT.

None exploreBiasFactor

The OPES-explore bias factor. Defaults to exploreBarrier / kT.

None saveFrequency

Interval in time steps at which to share the bias on disk.

None biasDir

Directory shared with other walkers. Each component uses its own subdirectory.

None walkerId

This walker's identifier within biasDir. See OPES.

None extraBias

Other biases acting on the simulation, as in OPES. They join the weights of the OPES kernels and of the free energy estimate.

None bounded bool

Whether non-periodic CVs have reflective boundaries. See OPES.

False warmupSteps

Unbiased steps for measuring the CV variance. See OPES.

None compressionThreshold float

Mahalanobis distance below which kernels are merged.

1.0 useExistingBandwidths bool

Whether the merge search scales by existing kernels' bandwidths.

True kernelShape str

"gaussian" or "compact".

'gaussian' statsWindowSize int

Window, in deposition strides, of the running CV-mean estimate.

10 minBandwidth

Per-CV floor on the bandwidth of new kernels. None by default.

None

The OPES and OPES-explore bias energies applied in a Context.

The explore part of the force is switched off for one evaluation of the bias force group, then restored.

The OPES and OPES-explore bias potentials on the grid.

docs.title: getCt
docs.text:
getCt(estimate='current')

c(t) of the total bias, V_opes + V_explore.

"current" averages exp(-beta V) over the free energy estimate of getFreeEnergy; "running" is kT ln of the mean weight of its samples, with an initial sample under the flat bias -(barrier + exploreBarrier). See OPES.getCt.

docs.title: getFreeEnergy
docs.text:
getFreeEnergy(correctSmoothing=False, pilotFactor=2.0)

Free energy as a function of the collective variables.

The estimate reweights every sample by the total bias, Eq. 14 of Ray and Rizzi. The grid and the smoothing correction follow OPES.getFreeEnergy.

docs.title: getNumKernels
docs.text:
getNumKernels()

Numbers of kernels in the OPES and OPES-explore bias estimates.

docs.title: getState
docs.text:
getState()

Flat, npz-writable snapshot of both components' accumulated state.

docs.title: setState
docs.text:
setState(state)

Restore both components from a snapshot.

The snapshot comes from getState. The restored bias reaches the simulation at the start of the next step, or sooner through updateContext.

docs.title: step
docs.text:
step(simulation, steps)

Advance the simulation by a number of time steps.

A CombinedOPES can also be passed to OPES.stepTogether along with other samplers.

docs.title: updateContext
docs.text:
updateContext(context)

Push the current biases into a Context.

Each table stores its component's bias shifted up by that component's barrier, so the unexplored floor sits at 0, as in OPES.

CVSpace(variables, bounded=False)

The domain of the collective variables: grid, periodicity, boundaries.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default variables

Sequence of collective variable descriptions. Each must expose minValue, maxValue, gridWidth and periodic; an openmm.app.BiasVariable qualifies.

required bounded bool

Whether non-periodic variables have reflective boundaries. When true the internal grid is tripled with mirrored copies on each side, and foldedGrid folds them back.

docs.title: foldedAxis
docs.text:
foldedAxis(index, values)

Fold one axis's tripled bounded profile back onto the domain, in log space.

A kernel factorizes over the CVs, and its mirror images under the reflective walls are every combination of per-axis reflections, so folding each axis's one-dimensional profile before the outer product gives exactly what foldedGrid gives on the full tripled grid, at a fraction of the cost.

Applies foldedAxis row by row.

docs.title: mirrorPositions
docs.text:
mirrorPositions(position)

Every image of position under the reflective boundaries.

For each non-periodic dimension, reflecting a point off both walls gives two images in addition to the point itself; the images across every dimension combine multiplicatively (a corner sees images of images). Unbounded spaces, or spaces with only periodic CVs, have no images: [position] is returned unchanged.

A kernel centered at any one of these images is, by the symmetry of reflection, exactly as far from a given query point as the original kernel is from that point's own mirror image -- so summing a kernel's density over these images is equivalent to summing the query point's images against the one true kernel, which is what the tripled evaluation grid does. Used to keep Kernel.evaluate (arbitrary points) consistent with Kernel.evaluateOnGrid.

docs.title: periodicCopies
docs.text:
periodicCopies(values)

Make the last node along every periodic axis an exact copy of the first.

The two nodes are the same point. Evaluating them separately can round differently (a matrix product, for one, need not give equal columns equal sums), and OpenMM rejects a periodic table whose ends differ at all.

docs.title: __iadd__
docs.text:
__iadd__(other)

Absorb every kernel of other.

The weight moments are combined directly rather than re-accumulated from the absorbed kernels: a compressed kernel carries the combined weight of all its samples, so squaring it would overstate the sum of squared weights and collapse the effective sample size.

docs.title: bandwidthFactor
docs.text:
bandwidthFactor(logWeight)

Silverman shrink factor for a new kernel of the given log weight.

Computed from this estimate's effective sample size with the new kernel's weight already counted, which is what update applies. The sample size also counts a prior weight w0 = 1, so kernels whose weights are small next to it barely shrink the bandwidth.

docs.title: getCorrectedLogPDF
docs.text:
getCorrectedLogPDF(pilotFactor=2.0, iterations=1, matchingScale=5.0)

Log density on the grid with the smoothing bias removed.

Kernel smoothing makes a density estimate too low on steep walls and too high at the bottom of basins, to order h^2 in the bandwidth. This applies the multiplicative bias correction of Jones, Linton and Nielsen (Biometrika 82, 327 (1995)), which cuts the bias to order h^4 while keeping the estimate positive:

  1. A pilot estimate P~ uses the same kernels, broadened by pilotFactor, which keeps its noise low.
  2. Each kernel's weight is divided by P~ at its center, so the reweighted samples follow P / P~, which is nearly flat.
  3. Smoothing that ratio with the broad kernels costs little bias, and P~ times the smoothed ratio estimates P.

iterations repeats steps 2 and 3 with the result as the pilot. The product does not conserve probability locally, which would shift free energy differences between basins. So the result is finally rescaled to carry, at the length scale of matchingScale pilot bandwidths, the same probability as the uncorrected estimate, which conserves it kernel by kernel.

The correction needs the broadened kernels to stay narrow compared with the features of the density, say a third of a basin's width. Early in a run, when the kernels are still wide, it can do more harm than good.

Only the reported density changes; the bias built from getLogPDF does not. Costs a few evaluations of the broadened kernels on the grid and at the kernel centers. NaN with no kernels.

docs.text:
getLogMeanDensity()

docs.text:
update(position, logWeight, variance, factor=None)

Deposit a kernel of the given log weight and per-CV variance.

docs.title: OPES
docs.text:
OPES(system, variables, temperature, barrier, frequency, varianceFrequency, biasFactor=None, exploreMode=False, bounded=False, saveFrequency=None, biasDir=None, walkerId=None, warmupSteps=None, compressionThreshold=1.0, useExistingBandwidths=True, kernelShape='gaussian', statsWindowSize=10, minBandwidth=None, extraBias=None)

On-the-fly Probability Enhanced Sampling.

Implements OPES and its exploratory variant, following Invernizzi and Parrinello, https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.0c00497 and https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.2c00152.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default system

The System to simulate. A CustomCVForce implementing the bias is created and added to it.

required variables

The collective variables whose sampling should be enhanced.

required temperature

The temperature at which the simulation is run.

required barrier

The free energy barrier the simulation should overcome.

required frequency

Interval in time steps at which to deposit a kernel.

required varianceFrequency

Interval in time steps at which to update the CV variance. When None, the bandwidth is fixed and taken from each variable's biasWidth, which is interpreted as the standard deviation of the UNBIASED distribution, exactly as both papers define sigma^(0).

required biasFactor

Defaults to barrier / kT. Must be finite: unlike PLUMED, the uniform-target limit inf is not supported.

None exploreMode bool

Whether to apply the OPES-explore variant. Must match the mode of a snapshot passed to setState and of every walker sharing biasDir.

False bounded bool

Whether non-periodic CVs have reflective boundaries.

False saveFrequency

Interval in time steps at which to share the bias on disk. Must be a multiple of frequency.

None biasDir

Directory shared with other walkers.

None walkerId

This walker's identifier within biasDir. Random when omitted; pass a stable value across restarts so a resumed walker reclaims its own file rather than leaving the previous run's behind as a phantom peer.

None warmupSteps

When given, run this many steps without depositing kernels while measuring the CV variance, then freeze it.

None compressionThreshold float

Mahalanobis distance below which kernels are merged.

1.0 useExistingBandwidths bool

Whether the merge search scales by existing kernels' bandwidths.

True kernelShape str

"gaussian" or "compact".

'gaussian' statsWindowSize int

Window, in deposition strides, of the running CV-mean estimate. With an adaptive variance, the first kernel also waits this many strides, so that it is sized from a measured variance.

10 minBandwidth

Per-CV floor on the bandwidth of new kernels. By default there is none, as in PLUMED, so that Silverman's rule alone sets bandwidths.

None extraBias

Other biases acting on the simulation, as PLUMED's EXTRA_BIAS: each sample is weighted by exp(beta (V + V_extra)), so that the free energy estimate removes them too. Items are force groups, Forces, or objects with a getBiasEnergy(context) method, such as other samplers. The bias itself still follows the density estimate as usual. In explore mode, only the reweighted estimate changes; PLUMED offers EXTRA_BIAS for OPES_METAD only.

None

docs.text:
addKernel(values, biasEnergy, variance=None)

Deposit a kernel into the probability estimates.

Returns whether a kernel was actually deposited: a non-positive variance estimate is skipped rather than deposited, since a zero bandwidth gives the kernel -inf log height and poisons the estimate.

This does not refresh any Context; call updateContext afterwards if a simulation is running.

NaN until the first kernel is deposited, like getFreeEnergy.

docs.title: getBias
docs.text:
getBias()

The OPES bias potential on the grid.

With no kernels deposited yet the estimate is empty, and both the log PDF and the log mean density are -inf, whose difference is NaN. The bias is well defined in that limit, though: the regularization term dominates, leaving the flat -barrier floor. Returning it explicitly keeps NaN out of the forces.

docs.title: getCollectiveVariables
docs.text:
getCollectiveVariables(simulation)

Current values of all collective variables in a Simulation.

docs.title: getCt
docs.text:
getCt(estimate='current')

c(t), the reweighting constant of the time-dependent bias.

Reweighting a sample taken at time t by exp(beta [V_t(s) - c(t)]) removes the bias even while it still changes. Two estimates are available:

  • "current": -kT ln over the reweighted density estimate P_n, for the bias acting now. It needs a reasonable P_n and is then unbiased.
  • "running": PLUMED's rct component, kT ln of the mean weight of all samples so far, including one fictitious sample under the initial flat bias -barrier. It averages over past biases, so it lags behind the current one. Like PLUMED, which warns against reweighting with rct, treat it as a convergence diagnostic: it should level off as the bias converges. With extraBias, the weights include the extra biases.

    • The current estimate is NaN before the first kernel.

docs.title: getFreeEnergy
docs.text:
getFreeEnergy(correctSmoothing=False, pilotFactor=2.0)

Free energy as a function of the collective variables.

Returned as an N-dimensional array in kJ/mole. The i'th position along an axis corresponds to minValue + i*(maxValue-minValue)/(gridWidth-1), matching the numpy.linspace(minValue, maxValue, gridWidth) axis the estimate is built on. Always the importance-sampling estimate, which converges better than the direct one in explore mode.

Every entry is NaN until the first kernel is deposited: with no samples there is no density to take a logarithm of. Unlike getBias, this has no defined limit to fall back on, and it never reaches the forces.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default correctSmoothing bool

Whether to remove the smoothing bias of the kernel estimate, which makes steep basin walls too low and basin floors too high. Uses OnlineKDE.getCorrectedLogPDF, a multiplicative correction that also lowers the noise of a single run, at the cost of a few evaluations of the kernels per call. Free energy differences between basins are unchanged. It helps once the kernels are narrow next to the basins, but early in a run, while they are still wide, it can make the surface worse.

False pilotFactor float

Broadening of the pilot kernels in that correction. Values of 1.5 to 3 work well; wider pilots leave more bias.

2.0

docs.title: stepTogether staticmethod
docs.text:
stepTogether(simulation, samplers, steps)

Advance a simulation biased by several OPES samplers at once.

Each sampler adds its own bias force to the same System, as several OPES actions do in a single PLUMED input. Each one deposits kernels on its own schedule and weights them by its own bias only. This is how, for instance, OPES and OPES-explore run together in OPES_COM (Ray & Rizzi, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 58 (2025)).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default simulation

The Simulation to advance. Its System must contain the forces of all samplers.

required samplers

The samplers acting on the simulation, all distinct.

required steps

The number of time steps to integrate.

required

docs.title: updateContext
docs.text:
updateContext(context)

Push the current bias into a Context.

The table stores V + barrier, so the energy the force contributes is the bias shifted up by barrier: the unexplored floor sits at 0. OpenMM's tabulated functions are zero outside their range, so a CV that leaves [minValue, maxValue] sees the bias of a region nothing has been deposited in, rather than a jump of barrier.
